skip_reason: Existing-move logistics only — not a sales call. This is an outbound pre-move confirmation call on an already-booked job, the same pattern skipped for this rep on 8/31 and 9/7. Chauny opens with 'I was just calling in regards to the move, of course on September 20th. Do you have a few minutes to just run through some details with me?' The move date, both unit numbers, the home sizes and the arrival window are already on file and she is reading them back for verification ('I do have with the arrival window between 1:00 and 130. Does that still work for you?'), and the customer already has a written estimate from the website ('the estimate I saw on the website was like 870'). There is no quote being built, no booking to attempt, no clock explanation, no differentiator pitch, and no deposit conversation, because the booking already exists. The only pricing content is Chauny restating the $210 hourly rate in answer to the customer's own question and then widening the already-delivered estimate from three-to-four hours to four-to-five based on newly verified access detail — estimate refinement on a booked job, not an estimate presentation. Grading it against the nine-section sales scorecard would produce a misleadingly low number and pollute the run average. Note: there is real coaching value in this call and a genuine estimate-accuracy signal in it — see the coaching note — it just does not belong in the scored set.
top_strength: Chauny caught a data error in the record that would have cost Einstein real money, and she caught it by listening rather than by reading. The file said first floor; mid-call the customer corrected her — 'Oh, yeah, so I'm currently on the third floor, it's not the first floor' — and instead of glossing over it she rebuilt the whole picture out loud: 'So, see, I'm looking at that too, so, here it, at first floor. So, okay. So there it is, it makes a little bit more sense. Okay, so we're on the third floor and then we have a little bit of a walk after we get off the elevator to your unit with and we got to make that walk [back] many times depending on how many things were loading up. And then you're moving to a fifth floor and it looks like this one is a bit of a walk as well. So, that makes a lot more sense now.' A job filed as a ground-floor one-bedroom is actually a third-floor-to-fifth-floor move with a roughly 150-foot walk from an elevator that is in a different building. That is the difference between a clean job and a crew running two hours over, and nobody would have known until move day. Her access probing is the best in the week's sample and it is the reason she found it — she asked what the parking looks like for the truck, she followed the customer's offhand mention of an elevator until she understood it was next door ('elevator next door. Like net elevator in like a different building I'm assuming'), and then she asked the question almost nobody asks: 'once they get to off the floor, I guess off the elevator. How far is your door from like the elevator?' She also handled a direct price objection without discounting and without defensiveness. The customer opened the call with it — he had moved for about $600 in three hours with another company and was looking at an $870 estimate — and rather than arguing she gave him the mechanism: 'you have to also think about what was that access like at the previous location that you were at,' then reframed the estimate as a truck reservation rather than a bill: 'with us you only pay for the time you use anyway. So while the estimate may be saying, you know, it's about three to four hours. If it does end up being the two and a half to three. That's all you end up paying for anyway, but it's more so for us to have, make sure that we have the truck reserved at an allowed time... so that we're not having to rush.' The customer's reply — 'Yeah, yeah, that makes a lot more sense' — is a fully resolved objection on a call that started at real cancellation risk. She was also straight and unfussy about EMMA rather than hiding behind it ('Sometimes she's a little spicy'), honest that disassembly is free ('it's not extra to disassembled and then put back together at the new place at all, that standard service for us'), and clean on the tipping question, which she answered with no pressure in either direction.
coaching_note: Not scored — this is a pre-move confirmation call on a booked job and it should be excluded from the sales average, same as this rep's 8/31 and 9/7 confirmation calls. But two things in it matter to Amanda beyond the grading run. First, the estimate-accuracy flag, and it is a real one. Chauny stated her own typical range out loud — 'a one bedroom apartment honestly takes about two and a half to three and a half is what we'd like to arrange that' — and then landed the reservation at four to five hours: 'we do have you sited for three to four hours right now... With this information, I would want to take this [four] to five for the truck reservation.' That is roughly 43 percent above her own stated ceiling, on a one-bedroom moving down the street with well under twenty boxes and no specialty items. Some of the increase is genuinely earned — third floor, fifth floor, an elevator in the next building, 150 feet of walk at each end — and she did the honest work of finding those. But she stacked the buffer on top of a range that already assumes an apartment, and she justified it with 'it's more so for us to have, make sure that we have the truck reserved' rather than with the hours she actually expects. Two separate numbers are now in play: what she believes the job takes and what the customer sees on paper. That is the padding pattern, just wearing a scheduling justification instead of a pricing one, and it is worth putting in front of the bottom-four group precisely because the reasoning sounds so reasonable. The coaching version: if the access detail genuinely moves the job to four hours, quote four hours and say why. If the fifth hour is truck-reservation insurance, hold it internally on the dispatch side and do not put it on the customer's estimate — because he will compare the paper number to the $600 he paid last time, and 'you only pay for what you use' has to be said three separate times to undo a number that did not need to be there. Second, this is now the fourth Chauny call in six weeks that the 85-point scorecard cannot grade, and the pattern is worth acting on rather than skipping again. These confirmation calls are high-value work — she found a two-floor data error and saved a blown move day — and none of it is measured anywhere. That is a live argument for the walkthrough-scheduler mini-rubric decision to grow a sibling: a short pre-move confirmation rubric covering verify-the-record, access detail, expectation reset, and a written recap. Worth raising at the calibration session with Cameron, Nhel and Tetet. Operationally, one thing to fix in the call itself: she promised 'I'm gonna send you an updated confirmation and this is gonna reflect just kind of the information that we've discussed,' which is the right instinct, but she never asked him to check it. On a call whose entire purpose was correcting wrong data in the record, the line 'take thirty seconds when it lands and reply if anything's off — especially the floors' is the one that closes the loop, and it was not said.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely warm and conversational throughout — 'I'm doing amazing. Thank you for asking,' an opening invitation for concerns before diving in, repeated 'does that make sense?' check-ins, and a customer whose posture visibly softened from a price challenge to 'yeah, that makes a lot more sense' — held back from a 5 only by circular, run-on explanations that take three passes to land a point that would fit in one.
audio_review_reason: Scored a 4 on warmth, but the transcript shows the customer's participation thinning noticeably across the back half — long Chauny stretches answered with bare 'Okay' and 'Mm-hmm' — which is the 4-or-5-with-a-possibly-disengaged-customer case the flagging rule calls out. Her delivery is also heavily circular on the page ('you know what I mean' as a recurring hinge, several restarted sentences), and audio is the only way to tell whether that reads as relaxed, friendly pacing or as a customer waiting for her to get to the point on a fifteen-minute call about a one-bedroom move.
